lessons.title: How doctors assess possible PsA

pages.body: There is no single test for PsA. A doctor looks at the whole pattern. This is often a rheumatologist, a doctor for joint and immune system diseases. They ask about your symptoms. They ask if psoriasis or PsA runs in your family. They check your joints, skin, and nails. Swollen or tender joints, psoriasis, and nail changes are important signs.

Blood tests help rule out other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis. X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI can show changes in joints, the spine, or where tendons attach to bone. See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back. Bring a short list of your changes to the visit.

key_takeaways: There is no single test for PsA.
See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back.

lessons.title: Understanding the CASPAR framework

pages.body: CASPAR is a set of rules doctors use to classify PsA. First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment. Then other signs are added. Psoriasis you have now counts the most. Psoriasis in the past, or in your family, also counts.

Nail changes count. So does a whole finger or toe that is swollen, now or in the past. A negative test for rheumatoid factor (RF) counts. So does new bone next to a joint on an X-ray. A heel spur alone does not count. A score is not a home diagnosis.

key_takeaways: First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment.
A score is not a home diagnosis.

lessons.title: What PsA is

pages.body: Psoriatic arthritis, or PsA, is a long-term condition linked to inflammation. The immune system becomes overactive. This can cause pain and swelling in joints and where tendons attach to bone. Psoriasis is a related skin condition that can cause scaly patches. Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition. Many people have skin psoriasis before joint symptoms begin. Some notice joint symptoms first.

The next lesson groups PsA into six areas, called domains. These are skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, swollen fingers or toes, and tendon attachment sites. You may have changes in some areas and not others. Not everyone has changes in all six areas. Skin and joint changes may follow different patterns. These areas describe the disease. They are not the six topics in this course.

key_takeaways: Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition.
Not everyone has changes in all six areas.

lessons.title: PsA across the body

pages.body: The six card labels describe different parts of PsA. Skin psoriasis means scaly skin patches. Nail psoriasis can cause pits or lifting of the nail. Peripheral arthritis affects joints away from the spine, such as those in the hands or knees. Axial disease affects the spine and may involve the joints that join the spine to the pelvis. These are called sacroiliac, or SI, joints.

Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe. Enthesitis means inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. The back or bottom of the heel may be affected. These six domains can help guide treatment discussions. They do not name a drug that is right for you. Eye or bowel inflammation can also occur alongside PsA. These are separate from the six domains. Heart health, blood sugar, weight, and mood can also matter in care. The symptoms topic covers these concerns and changes over time.

key_takeaways: Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe.
These six domains can help guide treatment discussions.

lessons.title: Skin and psoriasis

pages.body: Psoriasis can cause raised skin patches with scales. The skin card on the map shows one example. Patches may appear on the elbows or other parts of the body. Skin changes are one part of PsA care. A skin patch alone cannot show whether a person has joint disease.
Tell your care team about new or changing patches and any joint symptoms. Skin and joint changes do not always happen at the same time.

key_takeaways: Skin changes are one part of PsA care.
Skin and joint changes do not always happen at the same time.

lessons.title: Eyes and symptoms that need prompt care

pages.body: The eyes card describes inflammation inside the eye. One name for this is uveitis. It can cause eye pain, redness, blurred sight, or trouble with bright light. These symptoms can have other causes, too. A body map cannot tell which cause is present.

New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Possible acute eye inflammation needs a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. Do not wait for your next routine visit or a reply in the app. An eye exam is needed to find the cause.

key_takeaways: A body map cannot tell which cause is present.
Seek emergency care for a loss of vision.

lessons.title: Related health and changes over time

pages.body: The statement above the body map says PsA may lead to lasting damage. Disease activity can rise and fall. A flare is a time when symptoms return or worsen. A flare and lasting joint damage are different. A flare describes activity now; damage refers to changes that may persist. There is no fixed sequence that everyone follows. Treatment aims to control symptoms and limit harm. Tell the team about changes in pain, swelling, fatigue, or daily tasks.

A comorbidity means another health condition alongside PsA. This is not the same as joint damage. Your team may discuss heart health, blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, weight, or mood. Some people also have eye or bowel inflammation. Ask which health checks fit your history. A higher risk does not mean you will get another condition. A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk. Share concerns so the care plan can address your whole health.

key_takeaways: A flare and lasting joint damage are different.
A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk.

lessons.title: Gut and bowel changes

pages.body: The gut card describes pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD, can occur alongside PsA. This is a condition that causes inflammation in the gut. A bowel change does not prove that you have IBD or that PsA is the cause.

Tell your care team about gut symptoms that keep happening. Note what changed, when it started, and how it affects your day. Your team may ask about your medicines and decide whether you need more tests. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help.

key_takeaways: A bowel change does not prove that you have IBD or that PsA is the cause.
Tell your care team about gut symptoms that keep happening.

lessons.title: Shoulders and reaching

pages.body: The shoulders card shows that PsA can affect a shoulder joint and nearby tissues. Pain may make it hard to reach up or put on a shirt. A sore shoulder can have more than one cause. The body map shows a place to discuss, not a diagnosis.

Tell your team which shoulder hurts and when the pain began. Describe a task that has become harder, such as reaching a shelf. Mention stiffness, swelling, or a change in how far you can move. Your team can check the joint and the tissues around it.

key_takeaways: A sore shoulder can have more than one cause.
Describe a task that has become harder, such as reaching a shelf.

lessons.title: Wrists, hands, fingers, and nails

pages.body: This card groups several changes in the hands. A wrist or finger joint may hurt, swell, or feel stiff. Swelling of a whole finger is called dactylitis. It is different from swelling around just one joint. These changes can make tasks such as holding a cup or using buttons harder.

Nail psoriasis may cause small pits, yellow spots, or a nail lifting from its bed. The photo shows examples of nail changes. Nail changes and joint symptoms do not always happen together. Tell your team whether the change is in a nail, a joint, or the whole finger. Mention any trouble with daily tasks.

key_takeaways: Swelling of a whole finger is called dactylitis.
Nail changes and joint symptoms do not always happen together.

lessons.title: Feet, heel pain, and tendon attachments

pages.body: Enthesitis means inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. The feet card shows this type of change. The Achilles tendon joins the back of the heel. The plantar fascia attaches at the bottom of the heel. These sites can feel sore or tender. The two pictures show the difference in location.

Tell your team if pain is at the back or bottom of the heel, in a toe, or elsewhere in the foot. Mention whether walking has become harder. Heel pain can have several causes. A symptom picture cannot tell you the cause on its own. Your team can examine the area and decide what to check next.

key_takeaways: Heel pain can have several causes.
A symptom picture cannot tell you the cause on its own.

lessons.title: Spine and SI joints

pages.body: Axial disease means PsA affects the spine. It may also affect the sacroiliac, or SI, joints. These joints link the lower spine to the pelvis. Inflammation in these areas can cause back pain and stiffness. The spine card shows where these changes may occur.

Tell your care team where your back feels sore or stiff. Note when it happens and how it affects sleep or movement. Back pain can have many causes. This map cannot show which cause you have. A clinician uses your story, an exam, and sometimes tests to understand the pattern.

key_takeaways: Back pain can have many causes.
These joints link the lower spine to the pelvis.

lessons.title: Elbows and nearby tendons

pages.body: PsA can cause pain or tenderness in an elbow joint or nearby tendons. The elbow card shows these areas. Bending your arm or lifting an object may feel harder. Pain near an elbow and a skin patch on the elbow are different types of change.

lessons.title: Hips and daily movement

pages.body: The hips card shows that a hip joint can be affected by PsA. Pain or stiffness may limit movement. You may notice that steps, walking, or getting up from a chair are harder. These examples help you describe a problem; they do not prove that PsA is the cause.

Tell your team which side hurts and what has changed. Explain how the pain affects your daily routine. Mention a new limp or trouble doing a task you could do before. The team can check the hip and nearby areas. Do not use the map to decide the cause on your own.

key_takeaways: Pain or stiffness may limit movement.

lessons.title: How treatment goals are chosen

pages.body: Treatment discussions start with what is active and what matters to you. The six disease domains help describe this. They include skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, whole-digit swelling, and attachment sites. The care team considers these domains together.

Goals may include easing symptoms, protecting joints, and making daily tasks easier. Eye or bowel disease and other health conditions also matter. The team asks what you have tried before. They review your other medicines, side effects, and what matters to you. A treatment plan is chosen for a person, rather than from one symptom alone. A medicine that helps one domain may not cover every concern equally. Ask which parts of your disease the plan addresses and how progress will be checked.

key_takeaways: The care team considers these domains together.
A treatment plan is chosen for a person, rather than from one symptom alone.

lessons.title: Understanding treatment groups

pages.body: Medicines have different jobs. Some help ease pain and swelling. Others aim to control the disease process. These are called DMARDs. Conventional DMARDs act broadly on the immune system. Biologic drugs target selected immune signals. Targeted synthetic drugs act on pathways inside cells. These are names for groups. They do not rank drugs from good to bad. Some drugs are pills. Others are given by a shot or through a vein. How a drug enters the body does not tell you how well it will work for you.

A drug is not right for every person or every disease domain. Some plans also include skin care, physical therapy, or help with daily tasks. The benefits, risks, and checks depend on the drug. This lesson does not give doses or tell you to start, stop, or change a medicine. Ask the prescribing team what your drug is for. Ask which checks go with it, too. Make a list of all your drugs and supplements. Ask about blood tests, infection checks, and vaccines that may go with your plan. Keep follow-up visits even when you feel better.

key_takeaways: Medicines have different jobs.
They do not rank drugs from good to bad.

lessons.title: Tracking progress and planning for flares

pages.body: Follow-up visits look at more than one sign of disease activity. The team may check sore or swollen joints, skin, and tendon sites. They also ask about daily tasks. Your view of pain and health matters, too. Minimal disease activity, or MDA, uses several measures together. It helps track care. It is not a stage of disease. A quiet skin patch alone does not show the whole picture.

If symptoms return or worsen, discuss a flare plan with the care team. A short record can note what changed, when it began, and how it affects daily tasks. Ask which changes need a call, which contact route to use, and what to do outside office hours. Repeated flares may mean the plan needs review. Use instructions agreed with your prescribing team for medicine questions. This general lesson does not replace your own flare plan. A useful record can include pain, sleep, energy, mood, and one task that was hard that day. Share patterns at follow-up visits. This can help the team see changes that a single visit may miss.

key_takeaways: Follow-up visits look at more than one sign of disease activity.
If symptoms return or worsen, discuss a flare plan with the care team.

lessons.title: The four pillars of daily care

pages.body: Four pillars can help organize daily life with arthritis: Nourishment, Motion, Mastery, and Repose. In plain words, these mean food, movement, coping, and rest. They are a way to plan a discussion about everyday needs. They do not replace medical treatment. This framework is a guide to daily habits. It is not a test of how well your disease is controlled.

Think about which part of daily life is hardest right now. Food choices, activity, mood, and sleep may each raise different questions. A practical plan can focus on a small change that fits your needs and abilities. The care team can help tailor it. Bring up barriers such as pain, cost, fatigue, or poor sleep. Daily care works best as part of a shared plan, rather than as a test of willpower. Start with one small step you choose with your team. For example, plan a short walk that fits your joints, or set aside time to wind down before bed. Notice how the step fits into your day. You can adjust it as your needs change.

key_takeaways: They do not replace medical treatment.
The care team can help tailor it.

lessons.title: Movement, coping, and support

pages.body: Motion means finding ways to move that fit your joints and current health. Activity plans may include gentle movement, strength, and daily tasks. A physical therapist can help adapt a plan when pain or reduced movement gets in the way. An occupational therapist can suggest ways to protect joints during tasks. Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change. Walking, swimming, or cycling may be options. Ask your team which activities fit you before you start. The source also describes strength work and tai chi. You do not need to try every type of exercise.

Mastery means building ways to cope with the demands of a long-term condition. It does not mean controlling every symptom by thinking differently. Pain, fatigue, and uncertainty can affect mood and confidence. Support from trusted people, a support group, or a trained counselor may help. Tell the care team when worry or low mood affects daily life. Asking for support is part of care, not a sign of failure. A quiet pause or slow breathing may help you make space for stress. These are coping tools. They do not mean that pain is your fault or that you should skip medical care.

key_takeaways: Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change.
Asking for support is part of care, not a sign of failure.

lessons.title: Food, sleep, and recovery

pages.body: Nourishment focuses on food and nutrition needs. Food choices need to fit your own health and life. Food does not replace your prescribed PsA care. A dietitian can help with choices that fit your health, budget, and preferences. Ask about supplements or major diet changes before adding them to your care plan. The food chapter discusses vegetables, fruit, and sources of protein. Use these as topics to discuss with your team. It does not mean one food can switch off PsA. The lesson does not ask you to fast or follow a strict diet.

Repose focuses on rest and sleep. Pain or worry may make sleep harder, and poor sleep can make the next day feel harder to manage. Bring ongoing sleep problems to the care team. Describe whether pain, waking at night, or daytime tiredness is the main concern. Plans for meals, movement, coping, and rest should fit together. The aim is a manageable routine, rather than a strict rule for every day. Try to keep a steady time for bed and waking. A quiet, dark room and a calm wind-down routine may help. Let the team know if pain keeps waking you. Ask for help with sleep rather than changing your medicine on your own.

key_takeaways: Food does not replace your prescribed PsA care.
Bring ongoing sleep problems to the care team.

lessons.title: Sharing changes with your care team

pages.body: Tell the care team about symptoms that are new, keep returning, or are getting worse. A body map can help you name the area: skin, nails, hands, wrists, shoulders, elbows, back, hips, knees, ankles, or feet. Mention fatigue and changes in walking, sleep, work, or self-care. A useful message says where the problem is, when it began, and what has changed. You can say, for example, that new knee pain makes stairs harder.

A body map cannot tell you how urgent a symptom is. The next lesson explains eye and gut changes to report. Medicine concerns and repeated flares are also reasons to contact the prescribing team. Ask your clinic for its phone number and office hours. Ask about expected response times and how to get help when it is closed. Keep your own care plan available. For urgent symptoms, use urgent medical services rather than waiting for a routine app message.

key_takeaways: A useful message says where the problem is, when it began, and what has changed.
A body map cannot tell you how urgent a symptom is.

lessons.title: Eye and gut changes to report

pages.body: Eye symptoms can need prompt attention. New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Guidance for possible acute eye inflammation calls for a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. These symptoms have several possible causes. An examination is needed to find the cause; the app cannot diagnose uveitis from symptoms.

Tell the care team about ongoing gut pain, bloating, or changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease can occur alongside PsA, but a bowel change does not prove that it is the cause. Describe what changed and when. Your team can decide whether another assessment is needed. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help. Do not wait for a routine visit to discuss an urgent eye problem.

key_takeaways: New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment.
Seek emergency care for a loss of vision.
